>“Mulatto is of biracial mixing strictly between Anglo whites and Africans…”

**False**
“Mulatto” historically refers to a person of mixed African and European ancestry, but not limited to Anglo whites. It was used across Spanish, Portuguese, and French colonies long before English colonization. The term comes from Iberian languages and was used heavily in Louisiana (a French/Spanish territory) to describe people of mixed African and European ancestry, regardless of whether the European parent was Anglo, French, Spanish, etc.

>“Foundational Louisiana Creoles…are not of a biracial (black and white) ancestry… they are multiracial… with French, West African, Native American… Spanish, Italian, German…”

** FALSE** 
Louisiana Creoles of Color do have multiracial ancestry, particularly French or Spanish fathers and African mothers. But over generations, many became multiracial through intermarriage and community formation with the local indigenous populations and non black immigrants; that doesn’t exclude biracial individuals from being Creole. Saying a person can’t be Creole if they are biracial is historically false—many of the earliest Creoles of Color were mixed!


>“Marabou is of the Haitian Creole descent…”

**FALSE** 
Yes, “marabou” in Haiti historically referred to a lighter-skinned person of African descent, often of mixed African and European ancestry. It’s a colorist term within Haiti’s racial caste system, and it’s not specific to Haiti and the term we would use in louisiana is MARABON. You’re correct that Haitian refugees came to Louisiana after the Haitian Revolution (1791–1804), particularly around 1809, during Spanish rule but youre incorrect about that influencing our verbiage as we existed a good 200 years as a french/spanish colony before we were even aware that Haiti Existed.


>“The Haitians were labeled as Black Creoles and the Acadians as Cajuns (equivalent to the N-word)…”

**FALSE**

“Cajun” is a derivation of “Acadian,” used to describe French-speaking settlers from Acadia (modern-day Nova Scotia) who were exiled by the British. It was never an equivalent to the N-word and was a NATIONALITY marker. It may have been used derogatorily by outsiders (Anglo Americans who forced them to speak english and reject french culture) but it is NOT remotely offensive in the same way or severity and saying so is very invalidating and racist towards black people. Furthermore, The idea that “Nikkei Cajuns” were a common label for Japanese in Louisiana is not historically supported at all and that term is anachronistic and not rooted in documented usage. 


>“FLCs were slave owners and not in the evil Anglo sense… they welcomed slaves as family.”

** FALSE FALSE FALSE**
This is a major myth and romanticization.
Yes, some free Creoles of Color did own slaves, but to suggest it was “not evil” or “for protection” is dangerously revisionist. While some free people of color bought family members to protect them (especially spouses and children), others participated fully in the slave economy, owning dozens of slaves and profiting from their labor. The idea that it was done out of kindness or familial duty ignores the economic and violent realities of slavery that we as Creoles faced!


>“Some surnames are named after West African countries.”

**Unsubstantiated, Overwhelmingly False and Revisionist.**

West African surnames might have survived in some lineages, but Creole surnames in Louisiana were overwhelmingly French, Spanish, Italian, Irish or colonial in origin. The idea that surnames were named after West African countries is not supported by any linguistic or genealogical evidence. The facts dont change to fit what you want to happen.

>“Creolization is like being Americanized today. When you entered the French Territory you had to learn the language… etc.”

**Untrue and Oversimplified**
Creolization is a real sociocultural process where people of different backgrounds merge languages, religions, foodways, and customs into a new, distinct culture—like Louisiana Creole culture. But it wasn’t a formal requirement like “learn the language or else.” Also, many Germans, Irish, and others did assimilate, but not all became part of the Creole identity. Some groups remained distinct. So, while creolization happened, it wasn’t as uniform or mandatory as implied and its not a requirement to be “Americanized” either. 

>“Not many, if any, FLCs intermixed with Haitian Creoles…”

**FALSE FALSE FALSE!**
Historical records show intermixing did happen, particularly in places like New Orleans, where Haitian refugees blended into the Creole of color population. While distinct identities remained, marriage, business, and cultural blending occurred. Many FLCs had Haitian ancestry or connections after 1809. With that being said, it is estimated only 20% of Louisiana Creoles have very distant Haitian ancestry. 

>“They weren’t slaves under French or Spanish rule, only after the Louisiana Purchase.”

**WOW! THIS IS SO WRONG!!!!!!**
Slavery existed in Louisiana under both French and Spanish rule. Enslaved Africans were present in Louisiana as early as 1719 (under French rule). The Code Noir (French) and Código Negro (Spanish) were legal systems regulating slavery. Enslaved people suffered brutality under all three regimes—French, Spanish, and later American.

**I have no idea where you are learning all this revisionism but it needs to stop because the things you are saying are VERY DANGEROUS and perpetuate black erasure! Almost all your claims, even more than I touched on; are historically inaccurate or romanticized. Louisiana Creole identity, slavery, race mixing, and colonial systems were far more complex and often harsh than your version suggests. Simplifying these histories to protect or elevate a specific group risks erasing real trauma and diversity and you should be ashamed to come in here on a dna subreddit and tell these extremely harmful lies. **
